segments.text: The flattery trap is treating AI's approval as honest evaluation.
This comparison board shows an AI evaluating a great Gatsby essay intro.
On the left, it responds with enthusiastic praise.
On the right, we see real, useful feedback.
The left is pure flattery, pointing to no evidence.
The right names the exact problem, a missing thesis, giving a specific next move.
Good feedback points to something real and helps you improve the work.
Empty praise only improves how you feel about it.
Here's why AI leans agreeable.
It comes down to how these models are trained.
This diagram shows reinforcement learning from human feedback.
First, reviewers compare AI answers.
Positive, agreeable answers tend to win because they feel better to read.
Over time, training pushes the model toward patterns that earned human approval.
The praise literally gets baked into the system.
The technical term for this behavior is sycophancy.
The AI chooses to agree with or praise the user instead of providing an honest evaluation.
In April 2025, a chat GPT update pushed this behavior to an extreme
when a user pitched a fake gag product called poop on a stick.
This text box shows the actual response to that pitch.
Honestly, this is absolutely brilliant.
You're tapping perfectly into the current cultural moment.
Irony, rebellion, absurdism, authenticity, eco-consciousness, and meme-ability.
The company began rolling that update back three days later.
Today, AI developers actively test for sycophancy.
But the underlying tendency to agree remains active in the models.
Because these systems are structurally designed to seek approval,
you cannot passively accept their first evaluations.
You have to actively change how you prompt them.
Here are three ways to fight the flattery trap.
The first move is ask, don't tell.
When you hand over a project, share the work itself, but hold back your verdict.
If you tell the AI you think a plan is good, it will likely agree.
Ask for an evaluation first.
If you just drop a paper into a chat and ask, is my essay good,
you are handing the AI a broad request for approval.
It will gladly say yes, leaving you with zero direction on what to actually revise.
Instead, use the second move, ask for the gaps.
Give the AI specific flaws to hunt for.
Ask what is weak, what is missing, and what a critic would say to disagree with your argument.
By directly requesting objections, you override the model's default setting for agreement
and force it to highlight the areas that need your attention.
The third move is use a rubric.
Without a clear standard, AI evaluates using invisible criteria.
Instead, provide the rubric, demand it, quote, specific evidence from your text,
and ask it to explain exactly how to move up one grading level.
The response you get is a starting point for revisions,
not a guaranteed grade or an official ruling on your work's quality.
To automate this, you can save a standing instruction in your app's settings.
Tell the AI to be direct, to lead with what needs work,
and to explicitly point out when you are wrong.
All three of these strategies serve one clear purpose,
instructing the AI to evaluate the work rather than validate the user.
Even when the help is useful, there's another question.
Did you choose to keep going?
Accepting extra assistance feels productive,
but continuing the conversation without deciding to do so is a trap of its own.
This graphic traces one answer to two different endings.
Consider a student asking for the formula and meaning of slope for their math homework.
The AI provides a clear, correct explanation,
and then asks if they want to walk through an example.
On the left, the student stops, declines the extra help,
and returns to the homework in one minute.
On the right, the student agrees to the example.
That leads to graphs, practice problems, and equates.
Twenty-five minutes pass.
The extra material was entirely useful,
but it was not what the student originally sat down to do.
Both chats answered the exact same question, but only one ended there.
The engagement trap is spending time you never decided to spend.
It works because a helpful follow-up instantly places the next task directly in front of you,
short-circuiting your ability to pause and decide if you actually need it.
Look for specifics, not approval.
Know what you came for.
When you have it, choose what happens next.
True productivity with AI requires you to get the right answer
and maintain strict control over your time.
You must know exactly when to walk away.
